title: Your Photos Leak More Than You Think — Strip the Metadata
description: Every photo carries GPS coordinates, phone model and a timestamp. Here's how to wipe metadata from images and PDFs in seconds.
excerpt: A photo taken at home with GPS in the EXIF is your address, handed to a stranger.
content:
You photograph a couch, post it on a marketplace, and wait for offers. You've also just published the GPS coordinates of your living room, accurate to a few metres.

EXIF metadata carries coordinates, date and time, phone model, sometimes a serial number. In PDFs it's the author name, the machine name, and the full revision history.

## When it actually bites

Marketplace listings. Rental photos. Screenshots dropped into a public ticket. A CV sent to ten companies. In every case the file travels to strangers — carrying more than you meant to send.

With PDFs the classic failure is the template filename: "proposal_client_ABC_v3.docx" sitting in the metadata of a document you just sent to a different client.

## How to strip it

Open [FileTools](https://filetools.eu), upload the file, run the metadata cleaner. Processing happens locally in your browser, so the content never leaves your machine. You download a copy with no EXIF, no author, no revision trail.

It handles JPEG, PNG, HEIC and PDF. Batch mode takes a whole folder at once, which is the only sane way to clean thirty listing photos.

## What to keep

You don't always want everything gone. Photographers usually keep exposure data and copyright fields and drop only the location. Pick what leaves — a blanket wipe isn't always the right answer.

## Bottom line

Cleaning metadata takes ten seconds and prevents a problem most people notice far too late. Make it the last step before anything gets shared — [FileTools](https://filetools.eu) does it in bulk, and it's a tidy way to prep stills for video work in [TubeVoice](https://tubevoice.io) too.
